item.title: We are working with what we can control, we are waiting for the Referendum Act - Justice Ratuvili
item.description: We are working with what we can control. We are waiting for the Referendum Act to tell us what we need to do as it will have the processes on how to run a referendum as we have never had one in Fiji. item.content:encoded:
We are working with what we can control. We are waiting for the Referendum Act to tell us what we need to do as it will have the processes on how to run a referendum as we have never had one in Fiji.

Chairman of the Fijian Electoral Commission, Justice Usaia Ratuvili has made these comments after fijivillage News asked him on what is being done to ensure that the elections management body has adequate time, and to ensure that things are not rushed when it comes to electoral or constitutional changes that may confuse the voters.

Justice Ratuvili s ays they cannot control when the Referendum Act will come in and other issues about the constitutional changes.

He says they are preparing based on the current laws which are the Electoral Act, Registration of Voters Act and the Political Parties Act.

The Electoral Commission Chairman says while everything is in flux, they are concentrating on the registration of voters because if there is a referendum, it is the same voters who will be voting.

Justice Ratuvili says for the referendum, the Constitution Review Commission must complete its work by the end of August, and that must result in an amendment bill that goes to parliament to amend the constitution.

If two thirds of the Members of Parliament agree to the constitutional changes, then the Electoral Commission is required by law to hold a referendum.

Justice Ratuvili says in order to do that, there needs to be a Referendum Act in place.

He says there was a Bill that was presented, and he thinks it was severely lacking and has been withdrawn, and hopefully it comes in the next parliament session.

He admits there are a lot of contingencies there so while that is up in the air, they are doing what they can, and they are registering voters and parties, recruiting people and getting the logistics in place.

Justice Ratuvili says the general elections is what they are preparing for.

Questions are being raised on possible changes to the electoral system and processes too close to the general elections.

When asked by fijivillage News, Supervisor of Elections, Ana Mataiciwa says they are waiting for the legal framework like the Referendum Act.

She says operationally, they are continuing to register the voters and parties.

Mataiciwa says they have 1,508 confirmed polling venues, and contingency plans are in place for elections material.

She calls on people to be rest assured that the elections management body is ready to register and also conduct awareness campaigns to ensure we have a big voter turnout.

According to the law, the last date for the Writ of Elections to be issued is December 24th 2026, and the last date for the general elections is 6th February 2027 based on the current term of parliament.

A journey shaped by resilience, compassion and a commitment to serving others takes centre stage on this week's fijivillage Her-Story with Temalesi Vono, as Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection Sashi Kiran shares the experiences that have defined her life.

Kiran reflects on the lessons that shaped her values, and she opens up about issues close to her heart, including violence against women and children, drugs, HIV, peacebuilding, and the importance of creating opportunities for vulnerable communities.

item.title: Health Ministry working to ease pressure on St. Giles Hospital due to increased drug cases
item.description: Navitalai Naivalurua · 28/07/2026 The Ministry of Health is working to ensure that patients admitted to St. Giles Hospital are there to receive the specialised mental health services the facility is intended to provide.
item.content:encoded:
Navitalai Naivalurua · 28/07/2026

The Ministry of Health is working to ensure that patients admitted to St. Giles Hospital are there to receive the specialised mental health services the facility is intended to provide.

Health Minister Dr Ratu Atonio Lalabalavu made the comments when questioned by fijivillage News on whether the Ministry is looking at supporting St. Giles Hospital staff, who have raised concerns about limited space and manpower.

Dr Lalabalavu says the growing number of drug-related cases has resulted in more people seeking treatment at St. Giles Hospital.

Dr Lalabalavu says the Ministry is looking forward to the opening of the new centre and acknowledges the support of all stakeholders in achieving this milestone.

He says the fight against drugs is not the Government's responsibility alone but requires a whole-of-society approach.

When asked about the challenges the Ministry faces in addressing the drug crisis, Dr Lalabalavu says its primary focus is treating addiction, as the Ministry is often dealing with the consequences of drug abuse.

He says while the Ministry continues to care for acute drug-related cases, it welcomes facilities such as recovery centres that focus on prevention, awareness and behaviour change.

Dr Lalabalavu adds that these are areas where the Ministry hopes stakeholders and development partners will continue to provide support

item.title: Taxi Association calls for tougher safety measures after attacks on taxi drivers
item.description: The Fiji Taxi Association is calling for tougher safety measures, including increased Police patrols, more checkpoints, in-car cameras and GPS tracking systems, following the assaults of two taxi drivers in Wainibokasi this month. Association President Mohammed Faiyaz says the incidents are concerning and could happen anywhere in the country, not just in Nausori.
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Taxi Association is calling for tougher safety measures, including increased Police patrols, more checkpoints, in-car cameras and GPS tracking systems, following the assaults of two taxi drivers in Wainibokasi this month.

Association President Mohammed Faiyaz says the incidents are concerning and could happen anywhere in the country, not just in Nausori.

Faiyaz is urging taxi drivers to put their safety first and not pick up passengers if they believe their lives could be at risk.

He says taxi drivers provide an essential service to the public and should not have to face the risk of being assaulted or robbed while carrying out their work.

Meanwhile, Police are investigating the matter and trying to identify the people involved.

item.title: People may not hear about drug operations, but we are doing it - ACP Vusonilawe
item.description: People may not hear about operations, but we are doing it. That is the message from Assistant Commissioner of Police Kasiano Vusonilawe on the Fiji Police Force's ongoing drug operations.
item.content:encoded:
People may not hear about operations, but we are doing it.

That is the message from Assistant Commissioner of Police Kasiano Vusonilawe on the Fiji Police Force's ongoing drug operations.

Vusonilawe says the the Force has not stopped carrying out drug operations but has changed its operational strategies as criminals and drug dealers continue to adapt.

Responding to questions from the media on the apparent decline in publicly announced drug raids, Vusonilawe says criminals, drug dealers and others who go against the law have their own strategies and plans to outmanoeuvre police operations.

He says that is why police also have their own strategies and cannot continue with one trend of operations.

INSERT: ACP on police operations 28th July

When questioned by fijiivllage News on joint operations with the Republic of Fiji Military Forces, Vusonilawe says there are certain cases where police and the military come together to work as a joint team.

He says they demarcate cases because there are cases of national interest and there are routine cases.

He adds that the joint team is not deployed every day.

The Assistant Commissioner also stressed that the Fiji Police Force cannot tackle the drug problem alone.

He says police need the assistance of the public by providing information and supporting law enforcement efforts.

He adds that people also need to become more security-conscious and not assume Fiji is the same as it was in previous years.

item.title: Consumer Council warns public after 35 complaints linked to four online platforms
item.description: The Consumer Council of Fiji is urging people to exercise caution when shopping online after receiving 35 consumer complaints linked to four online platforms believed to be operated by the same individual. The Council says the complaints involve Trend Fiji with 15 complaints, Entertainment Hub/Playhub with 16 complaints, Pacific Closet with 2 complaints and Pacifika Playhub with 2 complaints.
item.content:encoded:
The Consumer Council of Fiji is urging people to exercise caution when shopping online after receiving 35 consumer complaints linked to four online platforms believed to be operated by the same individual.

The Council says the complaints involve Trend Fiji with 15 complaints, Entertainment Hub/Playhub with 16 complaints, Pacific Closet with 2 complaints and Pacifika Playhub with 2 complaints.

According to the Council, consumers reported responding to social media advertisements promoting a range of products and making full payment upfront.

However, they allege that the promised goods were never delivered.

The Council says consumers also claim their attempts to obtain updates or secure refunds were either ignored or met with repeated assurances that were never fulfilled.

Consumer Council of Fiji Chief Executive Officer Seema Shandil says the increasing number of complaints is concerning and should serve as a reminder for consumers to exercise caution when shopping online.

Shandil says while online shopping offers convenience and greater choice, consumers should not assume an online business is legitimate simply because it has an active social media presence.

The Council is advising consumers to verify sellers before making payments, check genuine customer reviews and ensure there are clear delivery arrangements and refund policies.

Shandil also urged consumers to be extra cautious when dealing with sellers who require full payment before dispatching goods, particularly where there is limited information about the business or no established track record.
